No, not really... it’s funny you ask that, actually, because people assume that all the time. My husband, for instance, he’ll see me pacing around the living room or shifting a million times on the couch, and he’ll ask, "What’s wrong? What are you stressing about?" And I always have to tell him, I’m not stressing about anything! 

I don't really sit around agonizing over things. I mean, sure, work is busy, and dealing with wholesale suppliers and shipping delays can be a total headache, but I don't take it home and fret over it. I don't lie awake at night spinning my wheels about finances or the state of the world or what someone said to me at the grocery store. My mind isn't filled with all these anxious "what ifs," you know? I've been a buyer for a long time, I know how to handle the curveballs. 

It’s really just this purely physical sensation. I can be in the best mood, completely content, painting a canvas and not having a single negative or worried thought in my head, but my foot is just going a mile a minute under the easel and I feel like I need to jump up and walk around the block. So, no, I wouldn't call myself a worrier at all. If anything, I'm usually the one telling my friends to stop overthinking things! Which just makes this whole buzzing feeling so much more frustrating, because if I was worried about something, at least there would be a logical reason for why I can't just sit still and relax, but since my mind is perfectly fine... I just don't get it.

Oh, absolutely. Yes, it’s not a new thing at all. Honestly, it goes way, way back. I mean, my mother saved all my old report cards and notes from teachers, and she actually just brought a box of them over a few months ago when she was downsizing. I was looking through them, and it’s almost comical how consistent it is.

I’d be talking over my classmates, interrupting, because I just had so much energy and the thought would pop into my head and I just had to get it out right that second. I remember teachers would be halfway through asking a question—like, they hadn't even finished the sentence—and I’d be rushing to answer it, practically shouting it out before anyone else had a chance to even process what was being asked. My parents tried everything, reward charts, punishments, but I just... I couldn't contain it. So, yes, that restless, buzzing feeling has been with me for as long as I can remember, really. It just looks a little different now that I'm an adult in a boardroom instead of a kid on a classroom rug, but the internal feeling is exactly the same.

No, actually, I don't really struggle with that. It's interesting, because I know people sometimes associate feeling restless with not being able to focus, but for me, those two things just don't go together. If I need to get something done, especially if it's important, I'm completely locked in.

========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Waiting my turn? Hmm... no, I don't think that was really an issue. I mean, I had—like I said before, I had all this energy, but I wasn't... I wasn't rude about it, if that makes sense. I understood the rules. 

I remember at recess, we played Four Square religiously. We had this huge blacktop behind the elementary school, and the maintenance guy, Mr. Henderson, had painted maybe six or seven courts in this bright yellow paint that was always peeling by the time spring rolled around. And there was always a huge line for the best court, the one near the big maple tree where there was actually a little bit of shade. I would stand in that line, and sure, I’d be bouncing on my toes, or maybe practicing my serving swing in the air, or just talking a mile a minute to whoever was in front of me—usually my best friend Sarah, she always wore these little plastic strawberry barrettes that clicked when she walked. But I never cut the line. I never jumped in before the person who got out was fully off the court. I knew exactly where my place was.

And it was the exact same way at home. We played a lot of board games on the weekends because my parents really believed in "family time" without the television on. Monopoly, Life, Sorry!... all of those. My older brother, David, he was always the banker in Monopoly, and he was so incredibly slow. He would count out the colorful bills, organizing them perfectly by denomination, making sure all the edges lined up. It honestly drove me crazy internally. I'd be sitting there tapping my little metal piece on the board—I always had to be the thimble, I just loved the texture of it—and I'd be squirming in my chair, practically vibrating while I waited for him to finish his turn so I could roll the dice. But I never reached over and grabbed the dice out of turn, and I never tried to go before he was completely finished. 

So, I guess the physical act of standing or sitting still while I waited was hard—my body always wanted to just go, go, go—but I didn't actually have trouble with the concept of waiting my turn. I didn't push ahead of people or anything like that.

It's just always there.\n\nDoctor: Do you also find yourself worrying about many different things most days?\n\nPatient: No, not really... it’s funny you ask that, actually, because people assume that all the time. My husband, for instance, he’ll see me pacing around the living room or shifting a million times on the couch, and he’ll ask, \"What’s wrong? What are you stressing about?\" And I always have to tell him, I’m not stressing about anything! \n\nI don't really sit around agonizing over things. I mean, sure, work is busy, and dealing with wholesale suppliers and shipping delays can be a total headache, but I don't take it home and fret over it. I don't lie awake at night spinning my wheels about finances or the state of the world or what someone said to me at the grocery store. My mind isn't filled with all these anxious \"what ifs,\" you know? I've been a buyer for a long time, I know how to handle the curveballs. \n\nIt’s really just this purely physical sensation. I can be in the best mood, completely content, painting a canvas and not having a single negative or worried thought in my head, but my foot is just going a mile a minute under the easel and I feel like I need to jump up and walk around the block. So, no, I wouldn't call myself a worrier at all. If anything, I'm usually the one telling my friends to stop overthinking things! Which just makes this whole buzzing feeling so much more frustrating, because if I was worried about something, at least there would be a logical reason for why I can't just sit still and relax, but since my mind is perfectly fine... I just don't get it.\n\nDoctor: Did you have similar trouble sitting still or feeling restless when you were a child?\n\nPatient: Oh, absolutely. Yes, it’s not a new thing at all. Honestly, it goes way, way back. I mean, my mother saved all my old report cards and notes from teachers, and she actually just brought a box of them over a few months ago when she was downsizing. I was looking through them, and it’s almost comical how consistent it is. \n\nI remember specifically in elementary school—second grade, third grade, Mrs. Gable’s class, Mr. Henderson’s class—it was always the same story. They were constantly sending notes home to my parents. And it wasn't that I was a bad kid or malicious, it was just... I literally could not stay in my seat. I’d be up sharpening my pencil three times, or walking over to the reading corner when we were supposed to be doing math, just constantly popping out of my chair like I was spring-loaded. \n\nAnd the talking! Oh my goodness, the notes always mentioned the talking. I would just blurt things out. I’d be talking over my classmates, interrupting, because I just had so much energy and the thought would pop into my head and I just had to get it out right that second. I remember teachers would be halfway through asking a question—like, they hadn't even finished the sentence—and I’d be rushing to answer it, practically shouting it out before anyone else had a chance to even process what was being asked. My parents tried everything, reward charts, punishments, but I just... I couldn't contain it. So, yes, that restless, buzzing feeling has been with me for as long as I can remember, really. It just looks a little different now that I'm an adult in a boardroom instead of a kid on a classroom rug, but the internal feeling is exactly the same.\n\nDoctor: Do you often have trouble sustaining your attention on tasks or activities, even when they’re important to do?\n\nPatient: No, actually, I don't really struggle with that. It's interesting, because I know people sometimes associate feeling restless with not being able to focus, but for me, those two things just don't go together. If I need to get something done, especially if it's important, I'm completely locked in. \n\nLike at work, for example. Being a buyer, you have to be so detail-oriented. I'll be looking at spreadsheets, analyzing sales trends for the last three quarters, comparing vendor pricing matrices, trying to figure out if we should increase our order volume on a specific product line for the holiday season... and I can sit there and just power through it. I don't lose my place, I don't get distracted and forget what I'm doing. My mind is totally focused on the numbers and the strategy. I mean, my body might be doing its own thing—like I said, my foot might be tapping a hole into the floorboard, or I might be clicking my pen a hundred times a minute, driving my assistant crazy—but my actual attention is right there on the screen. \n\nAnd it's the same thing at home. If I'm paying bills or reading a contract for some home repairs we're having done, I don't drift off. I read every line, I get it done. Even with my painting, which is supposed to be my relaxation time... I can focus on mixing the exact right shade of blue for the sky for twenty minutes straight. I don't lose my train of thought or forget what I was trying to accomplish. So, no, my attention span is actually really good. It's just my body that refuses to cooperate and stay still while my brain is doing all the focusing!\n\nDoctor: Do you often lose things you need for tasks or activities, like keys, your phone, or paperwork?\n\nPatient: No, not really. I mean, I'm pretty organized, honestly. I have to be, with my job. You can't be a buyer for a major retail chain and be constantly misplacing your purchase orders or losing your vendor contacts, right? It would be a disaster. So, I have systems. \n\nAt home, it's the same thing. My husband and I have this beautiful little ceramic bowl right by the front door—we bought it on a trip to Santa Fe a few years ago, it has this gorgeous turquoise glaze—and the rule is, the minute you walk in, the keys go in the bowl. Always. I never have to spend twenty minutes tearing the house apart looking for my car keys because they are always right there in the turquoise bowl. \n\nAnd my phone... well, it's practically glued to my hand anyway because of work emails, but if I do set it down, it's usually on the kitchen island or my nightstand. I'm just not one of those people who leaves their phone in the refrigerator or something crazy like that. I know some people are like that, and I always wonder how they function! But for me, everything has a place. Paperwork goes into the filing cabinet in the home office—I have it all color-coded by year and category, which probably sounds a little intense, but it saves so much time when tax season rolls around. So, no, I don't really lose things. I might be pacing around the house while I'm on a conference call, but I know exactly where my notes are.\n\nDoctor: Before age 12, did teachers or parents ever say you had trouble paying attention or seemed easily distracted?\n\nPatient: No, not that I can remember, and certainly not in those report cards I mentioned earlier. I mean, my mother and I sat at her kitchen table—she has this lovely little breakfast nook that looks out over her garden—and we went through practically every single piece of paper from kindergarten through, gosh, probably eighth grade. And while there were plenty of notes about me needing to stay in my seat, or talking too much, or being a \"chatterbox,\" which was Mrs. Gable's favorite word for me... there was never anything about me not paying attention. \n\nIn fact, it was usually the opposite. I was paying attention to everything. I knew exactly what the teacher was saying, which is why I'd blurt out the answers before she even finished asking the question! I wasn't daydreaming or staring out the window or forgetting what we were doing. I was just... doing it very loudly and with a lot of movement. I remember one time in fourth grade, we were doing a unit on the solar system, and I had built this whole diorama in a shoebox—painted the inside black, hung the little styrofoam planets from fishing line—and I was so focused on it, I practically memorized the encyclopedia entry for Jupiter. I just couldn't sit still while I was presenting it to the class. So, no, the distraction or inattention piece just wasn't there. It was always just the physical energy and the talking.\n\nDoctor: Before age 12, did you also have a lot of trouble waiting your turn?\n\nPatient: Waiting my turn? Hmm... no, I don't think that was really an issue. I mean, I had—like I said before, I had all this energy, but I wasn't... I wasn't rude about it, if that makes sense. I understood the rules. \n\nI remember at recess, we played Four Square religiously. We had this huge blacktop behind the elementary school, and the maintenance guy, Mr. Henderson, had painted maybe six or seven courts in this bright yellow paint that was always peeling by the time spring rolled around. And there was always a huge line for the best court, the one near the big maple tree where there was actually a little bit of shade. I would stand in that line, and sure, I’d be bouncing on my toes, or maybe practicing my serving swing in the air, or just talking a mile a minute to whoever was in front of me—usually my best friend Sarah, she always wore these little plastic strawberry barrettes that clicked when she walked. But I never cut the line. I never jumped in before the person who got out was fully off the court. I knew exactly where my place was.\n\nAnd it was the exact same way at home. My older brother, David, he was always the banker in Monopoly, and he was so incredibly slow. He would count out the colorful bills, organizing them perfectly by denomination, making sure all the edges lined up. It honestly drove me crazy internally. I'd be sitting there tapping my little metal piece on the board—I always had to be the thimble, I just loved the texture of it—and I'd be squirming in my chair, practically vibrating while I waited for him to finish his turn so I could roll the dice. Well, I suppose they have caused some issues, yes. Not disastrous ones, but... well, let me explain. At work, for example, I’m constantly moving, constantly talking, always needing to be doing something. And when I'm reviewing purchase orders—which, as a buyer, is a huge part of my day—I'm usually pacing around my office, or bouncing my leg under the desk, or just rushing through things because I feel this overwhelming need to get to the next task. And because of that rushing and that constant motion, I've made mistakes. I'll miss a detail, or I'll approve something too quickly, and it has led to corrected purchase orders. More than a few times, honestly. It got to the point where my planning coordinator, Jessica—she's wonderful, very detail-oriented, always wears these perfectly coordinated outfits—she actually had to start doing extra reviews of my work. Which is a little embarrassing, frankly, at my level, to have someone double-checking my purchase orders because I couldn't just sit still and focus on them properly the first time.

And then at home... well, it’s mostly around dinner time. We always try to sit down together, my husband and our two teenagers, around the dining room table. Well, yes, exactly like I was just saying about the purchase orders. It’s exactly that. And Jessica is so sweet about it, she never makes a big production out of it, she just highlights it in yellow and sends it back. Oh, absolutely. It’s funny you ask about trying to relax, because my husband brings this up all the time. He actually jokes that my version of relaxing is just doing different work in a different room. Even on weekends, when I’m supposed to be taking it easy and just unwinding from the week, I really struggle to just... stop. 

I’ll wake up on a Saturday, and I’ll tell myself, "Okay, today I am just going to sit on the patio with a book." But then I’ll finish my morning coffee, and immediately I’m up starting a load of laundry. And while the washer is running, I’ll think, "I should just quickly check my work emails," because, you know, some of our overseas vendors operate on different time zones and I just want to make sure there aren't any fires to put out. So I'm doing that, and then I’ll wander into the home office and see a box of product samples I brought home—maybe some of those ceramic goods from Gary in Ohio, or some new fabric swatches—and I’ll just start completely reorganizing them. I'll get them all laid out on the floor, sorting them by seasonal palette. 

And then, before I've even finished putting those away, I'll walk past the spare room and end up pulling out my easel to touch up a painting. I do a little bit of acrylic painting on the side, just landscapes mostly, but I’ll see a spot on a canvas where the shading is slightly off, and I just have to fix it right then and there. I literally just finish one thing and immediately pivot to start another, without even pausing to take a breath. 

My husband—who is a very calm, methodical person, he can just sit in his recliner and watch a three-hour historical documentary without moving a muscle—he just watches me bouncing around the house and he says I never really power down. He’ll say, "Honey, just sit down and watch this with me for five minutes," but I... I just can't. If I force myself to just sit there on the sofa, I feel this sort of humming energy in my limbs, like a motor running on idle. It’s almost more physically exhausting for me to try and stay still than it is to just get up and reorganize the linen closet. So, yes, I am constantly in motion, from the minute I wake up until my head finally hits the pillow.

She'll catch that I transposed a SKU number, which is an absolute nightmare because then the warehouse is expecting one thing and receives the wrong item entirely, and it throws off our whole seasonal inventory count. Or she'll see that I missed a freight surcharge that was buried in one of the columns, or that I carried the wrong quantity into the final purchase order. \n\nAnd it's just so frustrating because I really do look at the screen, and I think I'm seeing everything correctly in the moment. But it's like my eyes just skip over the fine print because my brain is already mentally moving on to the next vendor or the next email. I just want to get it done and get it out the door. It's not that I don't know how to do my job—I've been a buyer for a long time, I know these spreadsheets inside and out, I know what to look for—it's just these silly, careless little slips. And Jessica is so sweet about it, she never makes a big production out of it, she just highlights it in yellow and sends it back. But I know it creates extra work for her, and it just makes me feel like I'm losing my edge, you know? Like, how could I miss a simple freight charge when I've processed a thousand of these? And instead of just sitting there and letting them work through it, I'll interrupt them. I'll just blurt out this whole piece of advice before they've finished speaking. And then they'll look at me kind of sideways, and I'll realize they were about to say, \"...but my scholarship requires me to take this specific lab,\" or some other really important qualifier that completely changes the advice I should be giving them. \n\nI really don't mean to be rude or talk over people. It's just like I have the answer right there on the tip of my tongue, and it feels almost physically uncomfortable to hold it in. The thought is there and it just has to come out immediately, right in that exact second, before I've actually heard everything they have to say.\n\nDoctor: Do you also have trouble with inattention or distractibility in everyday life, not just restlessness and impulsivity?\n\nPatient: Oh, definitely. It’s not just the jumping out of my chair or the blurting things out. And then I have to sit there and awkwardly ask them to repeat the whole thing. It makes me look so unprofessional, like I don't care about what my colleagues are saying, which isn't true at all! I just literally cannot keep my attention anchored to their words.\n\nAnd it happens at home, too, which honestly makes me feel even worse. I'll just catch the very tail end of it, like \"...so what do you think I should do?\" And I just sit there, totally blank, feeling like the worst mother in the world, having to admit that I need her to say it all over again. Well, actually, now that you mention the inattention part... yes. I really have been noticing that, especially over the last couple of years. It’s incredibly frustrating because I’ve always prided myself on being able to juggle a million things at once, but lately... well, it’s the paperwork that's really tripping me up.

Oh, gosh, yes. Now that you frame it exactly like that... yes, I absolutely do still do that. It's actually a bit of a running issue for me, though I suppose it looks a little more professional now than it did when I was eight. 

Like, okay, in my vendor negotiations—you know, I mentioned Gary earlier, but it happens with a lot of our suppliers, especially the ones I've worked with for years. We'll be sitting there, maybe going over the seasonal pricing tiers or discussing freight options, and they'll start asking a question about our volume requirements. And because I know the catalog and our budget so well, my brain just jumps five steps ahead. I will literally jump right in with an answer before they've even finished their sentence. I'll just blurt out, "Yes, we can take the whole lot at that price point," or whatever it is I think they're asking. 

But then... well, then I realize I completely missed a really important qualifier they were about to add. Like, they were actually going to say, "Can you take the whole lot, *if* we have to delay the shipping container by three weeks?" And by then, I've already blurted out my answer, and I have to awkwardly backtrack and say, "Oh, wait, no, I didn't hear that last part," which is just terrible for negotiating leverage, let me tell you. It makes me look so eager and unpolished.

And it's not just at work, either. I also do this volunteer STEM mentoring—it's this really wonderful program for high school girls who are interested in analytics and supply chain management, which I think is just so important to get young women into these fields early on, you know? But anyway, I do the exact same thing with my mentees. A student will be asking me a question about a data set or a case study we're looking at, and I just get so excited to help or so eager to share my experience that I shoot out the answer before they're done speaking. And then, sure enough, I realize they had a specific "but what if..." qualifier at the end of their question that I just totally didn't wait to hear. So I end up answering a question they weren't even really asking. So, yes, the interrupting and the blurting things out is definitely still there, just... playing out in conference rooms and mentoring sessions instead of Mrs. Gable's math class.
